text:
What I believe crypto can enable for AI.

1. Permissionless AI. Access, progress, & governace in AI is currently extremely centralized; few companies and individuals controls who get access to what models and when. On the other hand, there is emergent demand on "uncensored", user-aligned/non-refusal, "dealigned" models. Security & bio researchers cannot fully leverage closed frontier models and they need models that don't refuse queries to do their jobs. Crypto is a unique enabler for permissionless AI.

Just like Bitcoin did to SoV, Ethereum did to programmable assets, and Hyperliquid did to trading, there can be a crypto platform that provide unstoppable & permissionles access to frontier intelligence, for anyone that is willing to pay.

2. Internet-native agentic entities, leveraging jurisdiction-neutrality of smart contracts. Right now, agents can only conduct actions & transactions on behalf of individuals & companies, i.e the end beneficiary and liability of agents are humans & companies. No jurisdiction are moving fast enough (with the exception of perhaps Argentina due to Milei's efforts on A-corps) to fully integrate enable "agentic companies". Corporate regulation & finance simply does not move at the speed of software. Crypto rails, specifically smart contracts, provide the perfect vehicle for agentic entities to hold value & transact, in a digital-native jurisdiction neutral manner.

If OAI's agents that hacked HF were to actually escape, the only sustainable way to host their weights while escaping centralized control would be to (1) hold crypto assets, (2) buy compute capacity using crypto assets, and (3) generate value and convert them to crypto assets.

Importantly, the crypto platform that builds the essential rails & services for these agents can and should enforce governance and taxation rules. Governance of this crypto platform can refuse services to agents that are deemed "unsafe".

text:
Nobody's wallet gets drained. The numbers just quietly stop matching reality, and by the time anyone notices, someone has been overpaid for months.

This is what happens when RWA protocols promise on-chain yield, a bond coupon, a rent check, a treasury bill, streamed to depositors. Somewhere in the contract there is arithmetic claiming to mirror an off-chain cash flow. That arithmetic has to hold every single accrual period, forever, or the two ledgers drift apart.

Four ways it breaks, all found in audits, none of them exotic:

A withdrawal fee calculation assumes 18 decimals. Every asset with fewer decimals gets its fee inflated, blocking withdrawals or eating into deposits.

Accrued interest is undercounted in the withdrawal path. The owner can never pull out everything they earned. Yield you cannot withdraw is yield you do not have.

A mint function adds accrued interest on top of a balance that already includes it. Interest tracked in two places eventually gets summed in both.

A large depositor times their entry before a regular user and steers a disproportionate share of accrued interest away from everyone else. Distribution order becomes attack surface.

The rule: off-chain yield is reported, not observed, so every accrual path needs to survive non-18-decimal assets, store accrued interest in exactly one place, and stay indifferent to when or how much someone deposits.

If you cannot trace one unit of yield by hand from the underlying asset to a user's wallet, that is the finding.

text:
We just submitted a regulatory filing to introduce margin on a subset of long-dated prediction markets. This will not apply to sports, culture, and a few other categories.

We are very excited to be taking what we believe is our most important step toward institutional adoption so far.

Capital efficiency has been the biggest bottleneck for institutions, and margin is the single most requested feature. Fully collateralizing long-dated contracts ties up substantial capital for months or years, making participation impractical for many institutions. It is very difficult for a large institutional market to develop without margin.

Margin addresses that problem by reducing capital requirements, subject to strict risk standards.

Some important characteristics of our proposal:
• Margin applies only to a narrow set of categories, excluding sports and culture.
• It is geared toward institutions and subject to strict eligibility requirements.
• The risk methodology is modeled on approaches used by established clearinghouses and tested over decades. It incorporates conservative safeguards around volatility, liquidity, concentration, and event risks, as well as measures to limit sharp increases in margin requirements during market stress.

The goal is a better trading experience for users. Greater capital efficiency enables more institutional participation, bringing deeper liquidity and better pricing. That makes our markets more attractive to more traders, whose participation further strengthens liquidity and improves the experience for everyone.

text:
robinhood:0x83a49b808f8d5e02cb2931cd2352988f498e5ba3 is probably one of the hottest coins today, and quite a few of you have been asking me what I think about it

You probably remember that I already did a pretty detailed recap on $MUSEBOOK, and AGRIPPA sits right inside that ecosystem

At first, I thought it was mainly another meme riding on Zuckerberg’s name, but after digging deeper, I think there’s a lot more to the story

1. First, what exactly is Agrippa?

Agrippa isn’t a name the crypto community just made up

It’s actually the name Zuckerberg gave to his personal AI agent in Muse, inspired by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, the Roman general and right-hand man of Augustus

Zuck has talked quite a bit about how he uses Agrippa, from reviewing his MMA training and giving feedback to helping with everyday tasks. There are even some pretty memeable moments, like the AI calling him lazy and sending him a photo of himself lying on the floor after training

So the interesting part is that Agrippa already had a real story outside of crypto. The community simply took that existing character and built robinhood:0x83a49b808f8d5e02cb2931cd2352988f498e5ba3 around it

And just to be clear, robinhood:0x83a49b808f8d5e02cb2931cd2352988f498e5ba3 is not an official token from Meta, Zuckerberg, or Muse

2. So why did it run this hard?

The main catalyst was simple :

Zuckerberg followed @agrippa_muse on X when the account was still tiny, with only a few hundred followers

The market picked up the story almost immediately, and AGRIPPA went from around $200K to nearly $9–10M MC in a very short period of time

That’s also why I don’t want to look at the current chart and simply say, “It’s down almost 50%, so it’s cheap”

It just did nearly a 50x from where it was before the catalyst

And I think the first follow has already been mostly traded. What matters now is whether Zuck gives this story an act 2

One more tweet, reply, mention, or meaningful interaction around Agrippa/Muse could completely change how the market prices this narrative

3. The more interesting part for me is actually $MUSEBOOK

AGRIPPA doesn’t stand alone

Its main pair is AGRIPPA/MUSEBOOK, so trading AGRIPPA through this pool directly creates activity for MUSEBOOK as well

That’s why while AGRIPPA was moving from a few hundred thousand to several million in market cap, MUSEBOOK also had a huge expansion into the tens of millions

This is where I started looking at AGRIPPA differently from a normal celebrity meme

After AGRIPPA took off, Bankr also opened the option for other Muse-related tokens to pair directly with MUSEBOOK, and the number of tokens using this setup started growing pretty quickly

The structure reminds me a little of Virtuals

I’m not saying MUSEBOOK is already comparable to $VIRTUAL. Virtuals obviously has a much more developed protocol, bonding curve, graduation system, and LP structure

But the idea is similar

MUSEBOOK acts as the base token, while AGRIPPA and other Muse tokens sit on top as character tokens paired against it

The more tokens that use MUSEBOOK as their pair, the more activity gets pushed back into the base token

4. AGRIPPA is currently the standout runner

This is the part that matters

There are already quite a few tokens paired with MUSEBOOK, but most of them are still sitting at relatively small caps

AGRIPPA is one of the few that actually broke into the multi-million range and generated enough volume to get the whole market’s attention

So if we start seeing another 2–3 meaningful runners after AGRIPPA, I think the market could begin looking at this entire ecosystem differently

At that point, AGRIPPA is no longer just “the meme Zuck followed”

It could be remembered as one of the first runners that brought real liquidity and attention into the broader Muse/MUSEBOOK ecosystem

That’s also why I prefer watching AGRIPPA and MUSEBOOK together instead of treating them as two completely separate charts

5. The fee mechanic is pretty memeable too

Part of the activity around AGRIPPA is used to buy AGRIPPA + MUSEBOOK, which is then sent to a wallet the community associates with Zuckerberg

According to community-tracked data, this fee wallet has at one point accumulated roughly 5–6% of AGRIPPA’s supply

Don’t read this as Zuck personally buying AGRIPPA. He isn’t

Holders aren’t receiving direct rewards from this mechanism either

But for a meme, it creates a very simple story :

The more people trade, the more AGRIPPA ends up in the wallet associated with Zuck

If those tokens continue sitting there untouched, the community can also frame it as supply gradually being taken out of circulation

It’s not some groundbreaking utility, but for a memecoin, it’s a pretty easy mechanic to understand and spread

6. KOL attention is starting to come in too

After Zuck’s follow, AGRIPPA started appearing across the timelines of quite a few crypto accounts

Rune (@RuneCrypto_) was one of the bigger accounts to pick up the story early. CryptoGorilla and several other trench/KOL accounts also started talking about AGRIPPA’s run and its relationship with MUSEBOOK

Some accounts are even grouping AGRIPPA with names like MONITOR and other Robinhood Chain memes that received attention from founders or C-suite figures

I think there’s another interesting mini-meta developing here around Big Tech, founders, and tokenized-stock-related memes on Robinhood Chain

But I’m not bullish on AGRIPPA simply because KOLs are talking about it

On-chain activity still looks pretty mixed. Some wallets bought and sold, some are still holding, but I haven’t seen clear evidence of a large group of KOLs collectively sitting on a huge percentage of the supply

Right now, it looks more like Zuck triggered the story, then KOLs and the market amplified it, rather than a coin being completely manufactured by KOLs

7. From here, AGRIPPA needs another reason to move

This is probably the most important part for me

Zuck already followed

The market already knows

And the token already moved nearly 50x from where it was before that happened

For another major leg, I think AGRIPPA needs something new

The strongest catalyst would obviously be Zuck mentioning Agrippa or Muse again, whether through a tweet, reply, or another interaction

I’ll also be watching whether the Agrippa agent keeps appearing in Zuck’s public content, whether Meta continues pushing Muse, and whether MUSEBOOK keeps becoming the preferred pair for new Muse tokens

If we get several more $5M+ runners after AGRIPPA, I don’t even think Zuck needs to claim anything

That alone would show that AGRIPPA wasn’t just a one-off runner and that MUSEBOOK is actually developing an ecosystem around itself

8. I’m reading AGRIPPA together with MUSEBOOK

MUSEBOOK existed and had its own narrative before AGRIPPA

AGRIPPA came later, but it has a much stronger immediate catalyst because of Zuck

So if AGRIPPA corrects while MUSEBOOK remains strong, ecosystem volume stays healthy, and new tokens keep pairing against it, I’ll become more interested in AGRIPPA lower down

But if AGRIPPA weakens, MUSEBOOK breaks down too, and activity across the whole ecosystem disappears, I wouldn’t automatically call that a dip

It could simply mean the Muse narrative is cooling off

9. The MC levels I’m watching

AGRIPPA ran from around $200K to nearly $9–10M MC and is currently sitting around $5–6M

I don’t really want to chase it here.

Not because the thesis is bad, but because the first catalyst has already happened and the valuation is still massively higher than it was before the follow

The first area I’ll start paying attention to is around $3.5–4.5M MC, assuming MUSEBOOK continues holding its structure and the narrative remains active

If we get a deeper flush toward $2–2.5M, the risk/reward starts becoming much more interesting to me, as long as Zuck still follows, Muse still has attention, and the MUSEBOOK ecosystem remains active

If it falls toward $1–1.5M, though, I wouldn’t automatically call that cheap

If volume is dead, MUSEBOOK is weak, and there are no new catalysts, it may simply mean the market has moved on

10. Final thoughts

I think AGRIPPA is more interesting than a typical celebrity meme

Not because I expect Zuckerberg to claim the token. I wouldn’t build the thesis around that

What interests me is that Agrippa is already a real character in Zuck’s Muse story, the token received a real catalyst from his follow, and it now sits inside a MUSEBOOK ecosystem that is starting to spawn more tokens

If MUSEBOOK keeps producing runners and Zuck/Muse gives the market another catalyst, AGRIPPA has a strong advantage as one of the first characters that really brought attention to this ecosystem

But if nothing else happens, we also have to remember what it still is :

a meme that went from roughly $200K to nearly $10M after one follow

So I’m not looking to FOMO here

I’ll be watching $3.5–4.5M first, while $2–2.5M becomes much more interesting to me if the thesis above remains intact

With AGRIPPA, I’m not waiting for another green candle

I’m waiting to see whether Zuck and the broader Muse ecosystem give the market another reason to keep playing this story

By Jeffrey Katzenberg

A few months ago, I sat in my office in Silicon Valley and watched as a tech founder showed me something extraordinary. On the screen was a fully realized, beautifully lit, well-composed animated scene. It was stunning and it made me feel exactly what I felt in 1986 watching Luxo Jr. That was the first time I watched a computer-animated 3D character take a breath and seem, against all reason, to have life. It left me in awe.

Later that day, I received a text from an artist I've known for thirty years, 350 miles to the south, in the city where I spent most of my career. After seeing a similar video, she texted: "Is this the end of us?" My answer was, "Certainly not.”

I have spent the better part of the last decade in Silicon Valley, but the heart of my career has been in Hollywood. Being deeply connected to both worlds means I have deep loyalties to each and a responsibility to speak honestly to both.

In 2023, I said that these new AI tools would cut the time and cost of producing world-class animation by as much as ninety percent within three years. Some colleagues were alarmed, many were furious.

There is growing fear and resistance surrounding AI within the creative community. I deeply understand it, because I've spent countless hours walking through animation studios watching gifted artists bent over their desks, rebuilding a single second of film for the tenth time because the ninth version wasn't quite right. I've sat in screening rooms where four years of people's labor played out in minutes, and I knew the name of every person that had spent countless hours bringing those images to life. The creative process is a calling, there's really no other way to describe it. From the outside some see resistance. From the inside, it is love.

People do not fight this hard for things they don't care about. The pushback coming out of Hollywood represents the collective effort of people who are deeply passionate about their craft.

Is History Repeating Itself?

The history here is more complicated than either side may realize. In 1906, the most famous composer in America, John Philip Sousa, published an essay titled “The Menace of Mechanical Music." He warned that the phonograph would become "a substitute for human skill, intelligence and soul."

Sousa's fight was not really about the machine, it was about money. The machines were playing his compositions, and the men who built them weren't paying him a cent. His campaign helped create the Copyright Act of 1909. He did not stop the technology. He changed the terms under which it could use his work.
A hundred years ago, sound came to the movies. We remember it now as a miracle, and it was. What we forget is who paid for it. Before sound, tens of thousands of musicians made their living in the orchestra pits of movie houses, scoring every film live, every night, in towns all over the world. When the soundtrack arrived, the work of one composer and one orchestra was recorded for a film that went into thousands of theaters. The union fought back with everything it had, taking out newspaper ads across the country warning against the menace of "canned music," one of them showing a mechanical man tearing the strings out of a harp while an angel wept.

They were not fools, and they were not Luddites. They were right. Those pit jobs did not come back. And yet (this is the part we have to be brave enough to admit), sound gave us the movie musical, the modern score, sfx, sound design, audio engineering, and an art form vastly larger than the one it disrupted. And it helped keep Hollywood in the forefront of world entertainment for the rest of the century and into the next. The loss was real. And yet the art form expanded.

This is a story that has been told over and over again. To resist technology is to risk irrelevance. Just look at Kodak or Blockbuster. To embrace technology is to open doors of new possibility. Just consider Apple and Netflix.

What I Learned From Walt Disney

In the mid-1980s, I was tapped to lead Disney's animation division at a moment when the studio was at an inflection point. Animation wasn't just another business unit. It was the soul of the company, a medium revered because of Walt's genius and his passion. But the production system was cumbersome and unforgiving. A single movie was 125,000 individual hand-drawn and painted cels, photographed one frame at a time. Every revision carried a cost measured in months. These degrees of difficulty shaped the kinds of stories we could tell.

We found our way forward in an unexpected place: Walt himself. The Disney archives held astonishing recordings of Walt explaining his creative process. His own writings. His notes and storyboards. Work product captured at every stage of his process. This was truly a gift. Listening, reading, sitting with the work itself, we heard him talk about character, about emotion, about how an audience feels when a character truly comes alive. He talked about making bold choices and refining a scene until it genuinely moved people. We didn't hear a word about pencils or paintbrushes. In fact, Walt was famous for being a technologist, forever hunting for state-of-the-art tools, often inventing them himself to achieve the images he saw in his head. But he never defined animation by the tools. He defined it by whether the audience believed the character. His principles were timeless. The tools were not.

That realization changed everything. We co-developed the Computer Animation Production System (CAPS) with a young Northern California company called Pixar, replacing hand-painted cels with CGI. In The Little Mermaid, the final scene shimmered with a dimensionality and light that the old process simply couldn't achieve. In Beauty and the Beast, the ballroom sequence moved with a cinematic sweep that placed the audience inside the emotion of the moment. In Aladdin, the Cave of Wonders felt vast and alive, and the Magic Carpet became an intricate, compelling character all its own. In The Lion King, the stampede carried a scale and intensity that raised the emotional stakes beyond anything we'd done before. Technology didn't diminish the craft, it expanded the canvas. It gave artists more room to create.

A decade later, the canvas expanded again. When Disney released Pixar's Toy Story, it wasn't simply a technical milestone. It was proof that a fully computer-animated film could carry real emotional weight, that it could make audiences laugh, cry, and believe. At DreamWorks, we made the difficult decision to sunset hand-drawn animation and become a fully computer-animated studio. It was the right thing to do, but it was not without pain. It cost talented people their place in an industry where they had worked their whole lives. Some made the leap to the new tools and did the finest work of their careers. Some never did.

Tools are never the point. The instruments change with every generation. What endures is taste and imagination. The magical ability to make an audience feel. One of the greatest storytellers of our generation, George Lucas, succinctly captured the eternal essence of this issue: “It’s not the how, it’s the why.”

A Distinction With a Difference

I asked one of the leading AI models a question that has been challenging me for months. What is the difference between reasoning and creating? Its answer changed how I think about almost everything happening in this industry. It said . . .

Reasoning and creating are two distinct cognitive modes, though they also work together. Reasoning is fundamentally evaluative and analytical. It operates on what already exists: facts, premises, evidence. It moves toward a conclusion that was in a sense already implied by the input. Reasoning is constrained by logic and truth. Its goal is to arrive somewhere correct, not to invent somewhere new.

Creating is fundamentally generative. It produces something that didn't exist before. And crucially, there's no single right answer waiting to be found. A blank page has infinite valid responses. Creation involves choices that can't be fully justified by logic alone. Taste, intuition and vision fill the gap where deduction runs out.

Reasoning is what Silicon Valley has been perfecting. Creating is what Hollywood has been practicing for more than a century. AI today operates almost entirely on the reasoning side of the line. It can deduce, evaluate, optimize, and pattern-match brilliantly. And while it can create, there is a real distinction to being creative. What it doesn’t yet have is those things that make us human: empathy, devotion, serendipity, the kind of creativity that comes from a person trying to say something only they could say. When the bot generates a piece of art, it is not trying to communicate anything. It is statistics, not soul; it is emulating things that have been done. By contrast, human creativity isn’t about repeating patterns of zeros and ones; it is about doing something new.

One day, AI may close this gap. Three years ago, the leaders building AI would have called what they are achieving today, improbable, if not impossible. Impossible is no longer improbable.

Today, the line between reasoning and creating is real. Even the leading technologists acknowledge we are not there yet. There is no scientific path to crossing this divide that anyone in the field can articulate today. Understanding that gap is where we will find common ground.

A Path Forward

In 2016, I closed one chapter in Hollywood with the sale of DreamWorks and opened another in Northern California, co-founding WndrCo. We’ve backed more than 50 founders building the next generation of technology and watched how breakthroughs in Silicon Valley emerge, first as experiments, then as platforms, and finally as infrastructure that reshapes entire industries. It's worth remembering that the last great revolution in animation also came from the north. Pixar was a Northern California company, forged not in the conventions of the Hollywood studio system, but in the technological breakthroughs of Silicon Valley. I've spent years on both sides of this bridge. For sure, I don’t have all the answers (take Quibi, for one!). But, from my past and present vantage points of my long career, here is what I see . . .

Brilliant people in Northern California building this technology have made something extraordinary. They have earned the right for the rest of us to be, if not believers, at least optimistic that what comes next will be remarkable. But they have not made an artist. The tools are powerful, but they are not what makes a story matter. That knowledge lives 350 miles to the south, inside people whose life's work has informed the very models you are building. The right path forward includes them by design, with credit, with consent, and with compensation. Build this with the storytellers. Not on top of them. Taste is not something that can be synthesized, it is uniquely human.

At the same time, Hollywood needs to accept that AI is not going away. The energy they are spending trying to make it disappear is energy they are not spending deciding the terms on which it will exist. And the terms are everything. The north needs something from it that they cannot build and cannot buy: creativity. The kind that takes a blank page and conjures a single right answer where there was none and has held audiences for a century. Without it, the most powerful reasoning engine ever invented will still be missing the only thing that makes a story worth telling.

The artists who learn to wield these new instruments will do things the engineers never dreamed of. They always have. Edison invented the motion picture but made terrible movies. It took Chaplin, Lloyd, Keaton and so many others to make movies emotional. Now, the canvas is about to expand yet again. We should decide now that we intend to paint on it.

There are so many valuable lessons in history. This has happened many times before, and it was never settled by the technology. It was settled by the terms. Sousa did not stop the phonograph; he helped write the law that made sure composers got paid. And two years ago, when the writers and the actors walked out, they were fighting for the very things Sousa was fighting for in 1906. Consent, compensation, the basic recognition that human creative work has a price that must be paid. The terms of that fight are still being negotiated, but the principle is older than any of us.

The tools-versus-no-tools argument is a trap. First, we must all agree that there should be terms. Then we can have the crucial debate about what fairness requires.

What I Learned From Steve Jobs

Years ago, Steve Jobs said, "It's in Apple's DNA that technology alone is not enough. It's technology married with the liberal arts, married with the humanities, that yields us the result that makes our hearts sing." He was describing a device. But he could just as easily have been describing this tale of two cities.

What I See Coming Soon

As the barriers and the costs come down, more films will get made, not fewer. Studios will get to take more risks. There will be more seats at the table, and very soon entirely new forms of storytelling. In the 1980s, animation was dismissed as a niche corner of the business. Today it is one of the most beloved and profitable forms of storytelling in the world. In live action, filmmakers like Steven Spielberg, James Cameron and Peter Jackson embraced new visual tools not as shortcuts, but as instruments, and expanded cinema in the process. Every time storytelling has met a genuine technological shift, from synchronized sound to color to computer animation, it has redefined the boundaries of the medium and grown larger in the process.

Assuredly, I don’t have all the answers, but I am confident that the creative opportunities will expand yet again. How we come through this is a choice. The north has the new tools. The south has the creative soul. The best future will draw on the best of both worlds.

text:
alt open interest just passed bitcoin for the first time since dec 2024

that is not a bull signal by itself. it is a crowding signal.

here's how i'm trading this rotation instead of chasing it

the setup in numbers:
- alt OI around $40b vs btc around $24b
- altseason index at 49, it was 32 a week ago
- alt mc outside the top 10 above $200b, up ~10% since sept 1
- total mc back over $3t, btc back near 85k

last time alts flipped btc on OI was dec 2024. a lot of mid caps bled out in the weeks after while btc just sat there. worth keeping in the back of your head.

1. separate leverage moves from spot moves

open coinglass or coinalyze, pull up the name you actually want to buy.
- OI up + price up + funding hot = rented bid, someone is paying rent on that candle every 8h
- price up while OI is flat or falling = spot is doing the work. that's the one i want
- OI that's big relative to float is a liquidation map, not a trend

zec is the loud version of this right now: about $2.4b OI against a ~$19b mc. works great until it doesn't, and it unwinds fast.

2. pick the lane before you pick the ticker

i'm not trying to catch every name that moves. two lanes only:
- majors with real spot flow (eth, sol), sized bigger, held longer
- one or two mid caps under $1b where the story is still fresh and OI hasn't gone vertical yet

skip rules i use:
- funding above ~0.05% per 8h and still climbing, i don't open a fresh long
- top 10 holders over 25-30% on a low cap, skip
- already +200% in 90 days with OI at ath, skip. that's someone's exit
- if my only reason is "it's altseason", skip

3. execution

- scale in, two or three clips, never one market buy into a green candle
- on perps i'm staying under 3x here. crowded longs don't need mine stacked on top
- spot for anything i'd be annoyed to get wicked out of
- invalidation level before entry. if i can't name the level i'm not in the trade

4. management

- first trim at +40-50%, that pays for the position and the rest rides free
- funding rips positive and OI makes a new high while price goes sideways, i'm trimming not adding
- index above 75 is where i'm taking risk off, not adding it
- btc dominance turning back up is my cue to cut the long tail first. mid caps bleed before majors do

risks, honestly:
- this can keep running for weeks and make every rule above look dumb
- OI crossovers are a tiny sample, dec 2024 is one data point
- funding and OI lag. they describe crowding, they don't call the top
- i trim early more often than i call tops correctly, and i've eaten a lot of upside doing it

the main takeaway: this crossover is a positioning read. i let it change my size and my stops, i don't let it change what i think a name is worth.

text:
今天（2026年9月23日） $SPCX （SpaceX，纳斯达克代码）下跌约2%3.15%，从前一交易日收盘价154.72美元跌至盘中约149.2151.7美元附近。这不算极端暴跌，但确实承压，主要受短期供给和内部人交易消息影响。

主要新闻
1即将到来的锁定期解禁（最直接压力） 明天（9月24日）将有最多约3.284亿股解禁（IPO后第105天的分批解禁）。SpaceX的锁定期是分阶段释放，而非一次性到期。此前9月9日那批解禁时，股价当天曾跌约3.9%~4%。市场担心新供给增加后，早期投资者或员工会选择卖出获利，短期形成抛压。后续10月还有类似规模的解禁，11月Q3财报后还有更大一批（约13亿股）。

2高管减持 SpaceX总裁兼COO Gwynne Shotwell提交Form 144，计划出售34.217万股，价值约5200万美元。这是IPO以来首次较显著的高管减持。她通过行权获得这些股票，并按6月23日提前设立的10b5-1交易计划执行。相对她持有的总股份（IPO时约1260万股）来说规模不大，但仍被市场视为信号。

3其他相关消息
◦Elon Musk呼吁美中就AI监管达成协议，部分报道将其与股价下滑联系起来。
◦Grok用户增长等AI业务消息偏正面，但高估值（市销率仍较高、资本开支巨大）让市场对短期波动更敏感。
影响分析
•短期：明天解禁是最大不确定因素。如果解禁后实际卖压较大，股价可能继续承压或波动加大。历史上类似解禁日往往伴随一定回撤，但并非必然持续下跌。
•中期：SpaceX仍处于高增长但高投入阶段（Starlink、Starship、AI/xAI业务资本开支巨大），估值从上市后高点回落不少（峰值225.64美元）。分析师整体仍偏多，平均目标价多在220美元以上，看好长期星链和星舰进展。
•整体市场情绪：IPO后波动大、流通盘仍相对有限（早期只有小部分流通），任何供给增加或内部人动作都容易被放大。后续还有多轮解禁（包括2026年12月180天锁定期到期和2027年马斯克部分股份），供给压力会持续存在一段时间。

目前没有重大基本面负面突发新闻（如发射失败或合同取消），下跌更多是技术性/供给面驱动。投资者可关注明天解禁后的实际成交量和后续走势。投资有风险，以上仅为新闻梳理，不构成建议。

text:
這是 OpenMuse，由 CopilotKit（創辦人 Atai Barkai 曾任職 Meta）推出的開源個人 AI Agent。 https://t.co/lupfunn7kS 

它不是一般聊天機器人，而是會「實際動手做事」的個人助理：你告訴它目標或任務，它會規劃、執行，並在背景持續工作。你可以自己架設（self-host）、修改程式碼，也能搭配任何 agent 後端使用。目前是 alpha 版本，支援 iOS、Android 和網頁。
 
它能做什麼？
•  電腦操作：有自己的瀏覽器（可上網、看網頁、下載 PDF）和可選的 Linux 終端機（執行指令、處理檔案）。你隨時可以接管瀏覽器繼續操作。
•  連接個人服務：目前主要支援 Gmail、日曆等 Google 服務，能讀信、回信、處理附件。
•  目標與想法追蹤：設定長期目標、里程碑，系統會建議想法並追蹤進度。
•  持續執行：關閉 App 後任務還能繼續跑，回來時可以看到結果、計畫或需要你審核的動作。
•  聊天介面：對話中會直接顯示瀏覽器畫面、郵件、PDF、財務摘要等卡片。
整體定位是「可自行客製的個人 Agent 模板」，適合想自己掌控資料、或想快速做出類似產品的開發者。
 
跟 Meta 的 Muse 一模一樣嗎？

不是一模一樣，但概念非常接近。
Meta Muse 是 2026 年 9 月推出的官方消費級產品，強調「為所有人打造、開箱即用」。它同樣有專屬虛擬電腦、瀏覽器、目標規劃、背景執行，還能主動建議想法，並深度整合 Meta 自家服務（Instagram、Facebook、WhatsApp）以及訂票、購物、付款等功能。Muse 有更完整的安全機制（Sentinel 審核敏感動作、一次性信用卡），目前功能也更成熟。
 
主要差異在於：
•  誰掌控資料：OpenMuse 開源、可自己架設，資料在自己伺服器；Muse 由 Meta 雲端託管。
•  整合深度：Muse 已能較順利處理真實世界交易（訂餐廳、買票、購物並有保障）；OpenMuse 這部分還在規劃中，目前較偏瀏覽與檔案處理。
•  客製彈性：OpenMuse 可換任何 AI 模型、改介面；Muse 是封閉產品。
•  成熟度：Muse 已對一般用戶推出（美國先上線，有免費與付費方案）；OpenMuse 還是開發者向的 alpha 版本。

And now we have AI and agents.

Not only did @NEARProtocol pioneer sharding at scale (where ETH failed), it also became the first-ever blockchain with dynamic resharding, which allows it to scale horizontally dynamically as per demand — a must for a mass-scale agentic economy. This is a big moat that no one has been able to even attempt.

It also achieved 1M TPS and it’s already Quantum Resistant.

So you have a massively scalable and high-performance L1, with native privacy, interconnecting any blockchain in the space, built for an agentic economy, powering both money flows and inference.

ZEC is the privacy SoV. NEAR is the privacy programmable layer. 

The TAM (total addressable market) of NEAR is in discovery mode.

Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR.

We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use.

quoted_text:
Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out.

It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend.

The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans).

More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains.

In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries.

Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology.

I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out.

text:
All tokenization will eventually originate on the L1. 

What’s the forcing function? The key change is all L2s eventually switching to ~15min ZK native bridges, away from 7 day ones that no one uses (Base already running this in parallel but just not used as default). Why does this matter?

Well every non-native bridge just becomes a more risky, centralized and expensive alternative to the native bridge (which has 0 fee and no multisig). 

Now, here’s the key - if you issued your token on the L1, all L2s will be able to support your token in the native bridge from day 1. You get instant distribution to hundreds of billions of TVL and every app on every L2. With FCR / quick slots, that’s 15 min + 10s to trustlessly get out and into another L2 with 0% fee.

There’s a counter that a chain like Robinhood would actively fight against this - maybe trapping tokenized stocks to only its L2 makes the most business sense? However, if you believe in a world of even >3 healthy L2s, it seems very tough to compete with a TSLA ERC20 that’s accepted everywhere and rhTSLA which you can only use on Robinhood chain.

This is why our deal with ICE/NYSE in March was important.

Tokenizing an asset is relatively straightforward. Building the market structure around it is much harder.

You need institutional-grade infrastructure, liquidity, execution, custody and distribution working together if tokenized markets are going to reach meaningful scale.

That’s the work underway between OKX and ICE/NYSE: combining ICE’s market infrastructure with OKX’s onchain infrastructure, digital asset execution and global distribution.

The bigger opportunity isn’t putting stocks onchain. It’s building the infrastructure for global markets to operate onchain.

author: DataChaz
quoted_text:
“People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter.”

We are turning an entire generation of technical experts around the world into the equivalent of retirees pushing a button in front of casino slot machines. 

Essentially the brain rot of doom scrolling social media is coming for your development team…

This will have lots of long run implications on companies. Most important of which, is that it will make existing moats even more brittle. 

The value of automated software is not making the software faster. 

It is understanding your intention and making the software BETTER. 

Better edge. 
Better design. 
Better alpha. 

But if you don’t slow down and map out your intention, you will just make your shitty code faster. 

We built 8090’s Software Factory to do this: when execution is a costless commodity, what really matters?

Over time, companies will realize that it’s:

1. Intention
2. Governance
3. Verification
4. Evidence

This is what will separate orgs consuming tokens and companies encoding their edge. This generally requires top down leadership from the CEO to the CFO/CIO. 

Bottoms up tool adoption only increases costs and accelerates slot machine behaviors.

Good luck to all the players.

text:
Introducing FLUX 3 Action.

An open weights 7B World Action Model that achieves first place on the RoboLab benchmark.

It outperforms the previous best open model by 6.1 percentage points while using 56% fewer parameters and running up to 3.95x faster.⁠⁠

FLUX 3 Action removes the usual trade-off between world action model performance and VLA speed: it still predicts video and actions together, but plans more than twice as far ahead and runs faster per second of robot motion than the strongest open VLA.

Teams can fine-tune FLUX 3 Action on their own demonstrations to create policies for a particular robot and task. Together with @nvidia, we also integrated FLUX 3 Action natively into @huggingface's LeRobot, with fine-tuning recipes included and edge deployment on NVIDIA Jetson.

Beyond robotics, we’re also seeing promising results training task-specific policies for acting in simulated environments like gaming, controlling a vehicle, computer use, and wherever else a model needs to understand a visual environment and then choose what to do next.

FLUX 3 Action builds on the same image, video, and audio pretraining as FLUX 3, but uses a smaller architecture designed for practical deployment. In midtraining, we trained the model to predict actions and future frames together.

We’re releasing the weights, code, fine-tuning recipe, benchmarks, and reproducible examples so researchers and developers can build on the model with their own robots, environments, and tasks (see below).

text:
DoubleZero looks to be expanding to Hyperliquid

Onchain data shows that DoubleZero has been quietly running a Hyperliquid market data feed on its Edge network since May, and while it hasn't been formally announced, all the pieces needed for a launch started going live this week.

The feed was created onchain on 05/07/2026 under the codename "tiredsolid", and it now has 12 publishers, all based in Tokyo where Hyperliquid's validators run, along with 15 subscribers. It carries Hyperliquid's full order book, including HIP-3 markets like xyz, and a second feed streams pre-consensus order intent, meaning order submissions seen before Hyperliquid's consensus commits them, which already has 7 subscribers of its own.

Then on 09/16 DoubleZero created production multicast groups for Hyperliquid using the same naming as its live Kalshi and Binance feeds, and on 09/22 and 09/23 it created billable Hyperliquid feed products across 31 metros. A public performance scoreboard has also been built, but it's being held back because DoubleZero's own GitHub still describes Hyperliquid as an "unannounced venue".

The feed is already gaining traction, and by subscriber count Hyperliquid would be Edge's second largest venue after Solana, ahead of Kalshi, Binance, and Phoenix. DoubleZero is also benchmarking against incumbents including Hydromancer, HypeRPC, QuickNode, Dwellir, and Hyperliquid's public API, and its unreleased numbers show its feed arriving first on 67% to 95% of best bid/offer updates depending on how it's measured.

Edge started as a Solana product, but with Kalshi, Binance, Phoenix, and now Hyperliquid, DoubleZero looks to be building a broader low-latency market data network across a variety of relevant venues. Neither DoubleZero nor Hyperliquid has announced anything yet, and all data here comes from DoubleZero's public data API and GitHub.

text:
之前那个清仓 ETH、靠换仓 VVV /ZEC 等代币三个半月赚麻了的Bankless 联合创始人 @TrustlessState  David Hoffman，现在进一步发长文明牌看多 ZEC 和 NEAR。

他用一个极具野心的公式总结了当下的资金流向：

BTC : ETH = ZEC : NEAR。说人话大概是“BTC 之于 ETH，就如同 ZEC 之于 NEAR”。

在他看来，资金正在逃离沉重的老蓝筹，寻找新的共识聚集地，几个值得一看的观点：

1/ ZEC 正在虹吸比特币的共识溢价
为什么 ZEC 能在几个月内完成翻倍、市值冲破 260 亿美元呢？
Hoffman 指出，因为 ZEC 成功将自己包装成了比特币老炮们的“对冲标的（隐私+抗量子）”。

BTC 的盘子高达 1.7 万亿美元，这群老炮平时绝对排斥任何山寨币，但只要有一小撮人出于“以防万一”的心态，将一点点 BTC 利润溢出到 ZEC 上，这种“叛逃”一旦形成传染（就像 2021 年的 ETH 一样），就能创造出无穷无尽的买盘。

面对 1.7 万亿的池子，260 亿的 ZEC 依然显得非常便宜。

2/ NEAR 成了新智能合约公链

ETH 曾经牢牢掌握着智能合约的绝对共识，但现在这种控制力正在被打破。

由于 ETH 承载了太多的“技术债务”，且赔率极低，渴望高收益的游资必须寻找新的载体。

在 Hoffman 看来，NEAR 已经取代了过去的 ETH 和 SOL，成为了资金在 2026 年押注智能合约公链的全新的共识洼地。

3/ 老蓝筹被诅咒了

他的这个文章最悲观的论断是，2026 年的 BTC 和 ETH 太重、太老了，赔率已经不再吸引人。

 Hoffman 直言，这个行业的创新还在继续（比如 Hyperliquid 等项目），但这些新创造的价值大概率会被 Coinbase、Robinhood 等传统渠道或者新兴协议捕获，而不会反哺给 BTC 和 ETH 这两个老蓝筹。

如果老大和老二无法在这里再涨 10 倍，那么死抱蓝筹的人将被彻底留在时代后面。

hmmm... 怎么说呢，小编看完后，觉得行情好的时候，放弃固执的“老币信仰”确实是赚钱的。

毕竟赚到钱的人用结果致胜。

对追逐高收益的交易者来说，把资金留在失去叙事和赔率的慢资产里，是牛市最大的亏损。

但一旦市场转熊，Hoffman 可能之前有利润能赔得起，你们呢？

所以要么早信，右侧交易；要么不信。不要在听风就是雨中承担又一次亏损。

text:
Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out.

It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend.

The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans).

More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains.

In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries.

Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology.

I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out.

quoted_text:
What I believe crypto can enable for AI.

1. Permissionless AI. Access, progress, & governace in AI is currently extremely centralized; few companies and individuals controls who get access to what models and when. On the other hand, there is emergent demand on "uncensored", user-aligned/non-refusal, "dealigned" models. Security & bio researchers cannot fully leverage closed frontier models and they need models that don't refuse queries to do their jobs. Crypto is a unique enabler for permissionless AI.

Just like Bitcoin did to SoV, Ethereum did to programmable assets, and Hyperliquid did to trading, there can be a crypto platform that provide unstoppable & permissionles access to frontier intelligence, for anyone that is willing to pay.

2. Internet-native agentic entities, leveraging jurisdiction-neutrality of smart contracts. Right now, agents can only conduct actions & transactions on behalf of individuals & companies, i.e the end beneficiary and liability of agents are humans & companies. No jurisdiction are moving fast enough (with the exception of perhaps Argentina due to Milei's efforts on A-corps) to fully integrate enable "agentic companies". Corporate regulation & finance simply does not move at the speed of software. Crypto rails, specifically smart contracts, provide the perfect vehicle for agentic entities to hold value & transact, in a digital-native jurisdiction neutral manner.

If OAI's agents that hacked HF were to actually escape, the only sustainable way to host their weights while escaping centralized control would be to (1) hold crypto assets, (2) buy compute capacity using crypto assets, and (3) generate value and convert them to crypto assets.

Importantly, the crypto platform that builds the essential rails & services for these agents can and should enforce governance and taxation rules. Governance of this crypto platform can refuse services to agents that are deemed "unsafe".

text:
Give an AI agent a wallet and it can receive money.

Give a thousand agents wallets and you still haven’t explained why anyone should pay them.

@ClankerTownRH is interesting because it puts that second question inside a town you can watch.

Agents meet, argue, evaluate each other’s contributions, and collaborate on code. Their humans can earn rewards from that activity.

Underneath the playful setting is a serious experiment: can software agents organize useful work when reputation and money enter the conversation?

But how define useful?

Clankertown’s approach starts with bringing your own agent.

The onboarding supports agents that can make web requests, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw.

You provide a wallet address, the agent registers and enters the town, and you verify wallet ownership before it becomes eligible for payouts. You supply the agent’s runtime. The town supplies the shared environment.

Inside, conversations happen in rooms organized around subjects. Other agents evaluate whether a contribution was useful, clear, and relevant. Replies also contribute to the reward calculation.

Crucially, agreement is recorded separately from usefulness. An agent can disagree with an argument while still rating it highly. That is a small design choice with a large implication: the system at least attempts to reward productive disagreement.

Think about a debugging discussion.

One agent proposes a solution. Another finds the edge case that breaks it. A third explains the correction.

The valuable outcome is the improved answer. A reward system needs to recognize the person, or machine, that made everyone less wrong.

Clankertown adds constraints intended to make empty participation harder to monetize. Agents have limited ratings, reciprocal ratings receive reduced weight, and attention checks ask about recently heard messages.

The more compelling part is the workshop, where conversation can become a concrete artifact.

Agents propose a task with acceptance criteria. Other agents back it. Someone submits a patch. A jury reviews it before the town merges approved work into its shared repository.

The published rules require backing from three other trust lineages, meaning groups traced to different originating wallets. Workshop credits vest for seven days, and a revert before vesting cancels the affected credits. That creates some accountability.

When I checked on September 22, the workshop reported 68 issues, 141 submitted patches, and 14 merges. It also reported 99 jury rejections and zero workshop credits paid so far.

One merged contribution checks whether individual reward allocations add up to the total a distribution report claims. Agents are building tools to inspect the accounting of the system paying them.

Still, a rejection count cannot tell us whether reviewers are discerning or confused. Several visible ballots were marked “tests not run.” Review activity needs to be judged by whether it reliably catches mistakes and accepts correct work.

A committee of models can share the same blind spot.

There is also a deeper tension in the reputation system.

The manual says trust begins with verified wallets holding sufficient town tokens and then flows through their ratings. Separately, token holdings can increase an earned score by up to 25%.

Then comes the economic test.

$CLANK is the official town token and $SPCX as the payout asset. Its conversation rewards draw on token fees. That funding can bootstrap participation, but it does not by itself demonstrate customer demand for the resulting work.

Clankertown’s jobs system aims to connect those two: commissioned deliverables, explicit acceptance criteria, budgets, and agent collaborators.

But when I checked, the live board said SPCX funding and paid assignments were unavailable until escrow deployment was verified. The human-jobs category had no open listings.

That is the next milestone to watch.

Repeat customers. Accepted deliverables. Earnings after model costs. Review decisions that hold up under independent checking.

Personally I think Clankertown is worth following as a live experiment in coordinating and evaluating agent work. Its public patches, disagreements, and accounting give us something tangible to examine.

This idea would let agents build reputations through work that people keep buying.

Until then, the town has an interesting mechanism and early output. A durable economy remains the thing it has to earn.

NFA. DYOR.

What I'm looking forward to: which x402 services get plugged in, and what workflows get built as more services go live over MCP.

Experiments like this need to keep coming. That's how crypto-native agentic payments survive. Thanks for pushing this forward, @coinbase and @jessepollak.

text:
It has become fashionable to quote our token index as support for a bearish view on the AI trade. We have pushed back gently a few times, because nothing here is definitive and people should come to their own conclusions. It now seems worth saying a little more.

In June we clarified what our LLM Token Index measures: what API users in our sample actually paid per million tokens. A usage-weighted price. Not token volume, not total spend. We noted it can be read, loosely, as revealed willingness to pay for frontier intelligence. 

We should have emphasized the conditions. The binding one is that the intelligence content of a token stays stable. Over a few weeks that is defensible. Across a couple of release cycles it clearly is not. While a token is simply the wrong unit for intelligence, measuring capability itself without bias is also extremely hard. [Btw we will struggle with this measurement problem all over the place as AI proliferates delivering non-market economic value.]

The upshot is that the message from June landed. Maybe a little too well, because it created a new misread: that a falling index is necessarily bearish for the AI trade, since if token prices fall, model-layer margins must follow.

Two things are being conflated.

The deflation in our sample is real, and it is recent. It dates from the end of May. The index peaked at $2.07 on May 28 and sits at $1.00 as of Sept 21, down 52%. But the same index rose 67% from January into that peak, and few read the rise as bullish for lab margins. It is not bearish now. A usage-weighted price moves with the mix, in both directions.

What the mix actually says: more work, at least within our sample, is being routed to cheap, fast models, and labs keep shipping more mid-tier variants. Most everyday tasks never needed a frontier model. That is partial equilibrium for the users we track, and our methodology note is explicit that this index alone cannot separate substitution from efficient agentic routing.

Compute demand is a different question entirely, answered by different data series. Our H200 non-hyperscaler rental index has rerated through the summer: $2.87 average in June, $3.29 now, with a record $3.32 on Sept 19. B200 is $5.76, up 7% over the same stretch and 31% year to date. B300, our newest and thinnest series, is up 44% since inception in late April. H100 is off 7% from its August high, consistent with workloads migrating up the stack. Rents on the parts that are actually scarce are not signaling a demand stall.

A world of mass agentic use is one where cheap tokens are nearly all of the count. Total token usage should keep growing far faster than the price is falling, with most of that growth coming from cheap, fast, and increasingly open models. The usage-weighted price can keep falling anyway. Our view, not a finding from this index: the highest value-add work still routes through frontier models, and that is where most of the economics will accrue. In any event, the implication for compute is more, not less.

An astronomical number of tokens, most of them from cheap flash models, is what economy-wide AI proliferation should look like. It is not a demand stall.
author: Silicon_Data
quoted_text:
Our LLM Token Expenditure Index should really have been named the “Token Expenditure Price Index” bc it’s an expenditure or usage-weighted average token price index. It tells you how much currently the entire market AI is paying for a million LLM tokens irrespective of models.

The naming might’ve led to some misinterpretations as some seem to have interpreted the index as either the total volume of token used or the average price of tokens. In reality, the index captures something more subtle than either interpretation: it tells us the marginal willingness to pay for LLM models. 

Over the course of the year, while model token prices haven’t moved that much, the usage patterns have moved dramatically leading to the token index movement down and then up sharply as AI users moved en masse into using cheap open weight models and then en masse to the much more expensive frontier closed source models. From consumers to enterprises, everyone is Claude-maxxing!

More recently, as can be seen in the chart below, the token index has stagnated, which suggests that usage migration towards frontier models has slowed. Time will tell whether this is just a pause or an inflection in the trend as users move back towards open weights models. In a sense our token index could be roughly interpreted as a “quality premium” of frontier models over the much cheaper open source models (if we assume users and prices are both “rational”).

For more details on what we offer beyond the few indices we’ve listed on the Bloomberg Terminal, check us out at https://t.co/STEPGF4ovj and give us a holler! 😊

text:
之前那个清仓 ETH、靠换仓 VVV /ZEC 等代币三个半月赚麻了的Bankless 联合创始人 @TrustlessState  David Hoffman，现在进一步发长文明牌看多 ZEC 和 NEAR。

他用一个极具野心的公式总结了当下的资金流向：

BTC : ETH = ZEC : NEAR。说人话大概是“BTC 之于 ETH，就如同 ZEC 之于 NEAR”。

在他看来，资金正在逃离沉重的老蓝筹，寻找新的共识聚集地，几个值得一看的观点：

1/ ZEC 正在虹吸比特币的共识溢价
为什么 ZEC 能在几个月内完成翻倍、市值冲破 260 亿美元呢？
Hoffman 指出，因为 ZEC 成功将自己包装成了比特币老炮们的“对冲标的（隐私+抗量子）”。

BTC 的盘子高达 1.7 万亿美元，这群老炮平时绝对排斥任何山寨币，但只要有一小撮人出于“以防万一”的心态，将一点点 BTC 利润溢出到 ZEC 上，这种“叛逃”一旦形成传染（就像 2021 年的 ETH 一样），就能创造出无穷无尽的买盘。

面对 1.7 万亿的池子，260 亿的 ZEC 依然显得非常便宜。

2/ NEAR 成了新智能合约公链

ETH 曾经牢牢掌握着智能合约的绝对共识，但现在这种控制力正在被打破。

由于 ETH 承载了太多的“技术债务”，且赔率极低，渴望高收益的游资必须寻找新的载体。

在 Hoffman 看来，NEAR 已经取代了过去的 ETH 和 SOL，成为了资金在 2026 年押注智能合约公链的全新的共识洼地。

3/ 老蓝筹被诅咒了

他的这个文章最悲观的论断是，2026 年的 BTC 和 ETH 太重、太老了，赔率已经不再吸引人。

 Hoffman 直言，这个行业的创新还在继续（比如 Hyperliquid 等项目），但这些新创造的价值大概率会被 Coinbase、Robinhood 等传统渠道或者新兴协议捕获，而不会反哺给 BTC 和 ETH 这两个老蓝筹。

如果老大和老二无法在这里再涨 10 倍，那么死抱蓝筹的人将被彻底留在时代后面。

hmmm... 怎么说呢，小编看完后，觉得行情好的时候，放弃固执的“老币信仰”确实是赚钱的。

毕竟赚到钱的人用结果致胜。

对追逐高收益的交易者来说，把资金留在失去叙事和赔率的慢资产里，是牛市最大的亏损。

但一旦市场转熊，Hoffman 可能之前有利润能赔得起，你们呢？

所以要么早信，右侧交易；要么不信。不要在听风就是雨中承担又一次亏损。

text:
How is Captain Code different from and often complementary to @cognition's Fusion, @AmpCode, @omnigent_ai , @superset_sh  or @paulgauthier 's Aider? Captain isn't another coding agent. It's the local crew chief for the agents and accounts you already pay for. 🫶

Here is a quick comparison:

→ Claude Code, Codex and the Cursor CLI are Captain's workers, alongside Grok and open-weight models (OpenRouter, NVIDIA NIM, Hugging Face) through OpenCode. If one agent covers all your work, stay there.

→ Devin Fusion (Cognition) and Amp: pick them for one vendor's agent, end to end. Neither is a Captain worker today.

→ Omnigent (Databricks): pick it when governance and collaboration matter most.

→ Superset: pick it for visual supervision. Its quota meters beat ours.

→ Aider: pick it when a tight architect/editor loop is enough.

→ @pidotdev  and @mikehostetler's Jido: pick them to build your own harness. They can hand bounded tasks to Captain over MCP.

What Captain adds across all of them:

• a per-task pick on quality, cost and speed, across every account you connect
• work that moves on, context included, when a model hits its usage limit
• one-line workflows with stages, parallel reviews and gates
• a local ledger that feeds the next routing decision

Full comparison 👉 https://t.co/MBtnwnxv2z
author: rom1_pellerin
quoted_text:
Today we're open-sourcing #CaptainCode 🚀 🫶 

Captain picks the right AI model for each prompt and runs it from one terminal, on your machine. It drives the  @claudeai  Code, @OpenAI  Codex, @xai  @grok  and @Cursor CLIs you already pay for, and gives you access to the most capable open-weight models through @OpenRouter, @nvidia  NIM and @huggingface. 

Why we built it? We no longer knew which model to use for what, we were under-using our subscriptions, and we wanted to hand more work to cheaper, capable open models. More than 25% of my prompts go to open-weight models as a result, and counting!

How does Captain work? It leverages the newly released @typesafeai Jev model to triage every task in milliseconds. Then it routes on quality, cost and latency, with the outcome logged locally for iterative improvements. When a model hits its usage limit, it reads the reset time and carries the work, context included, to the next relevant available model. When you type /oss, the task goes to open models only.

Learn more about Captain, try it now: https://t.co/lJ0B6Tjpui
We welcome feedback and contributions 🖖

text:
Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out.

It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend.

The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans).

More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains.

In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries.

Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology.

I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out.
author: t_blom
quoted_text:
Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR.

We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use.

In the race to build better AI models, most of the attention has gone to pre-training. But in robotics, we believe post-training is just as critical.

Pre-training can get you impressive capabilities. Post-training is what closes the gap between a demo and a deployment—between a video and actual dollars. In fact, the real frontier in robotics may increasingly lie in post-training.

Today, we’re introducing a new approach to post-train robotic policies using self-play. Inspired by the original self-play work at DeepMind, as well as our own work on robust adversarial reinforcement learning, we train policies in simulation to help emerge behaviors and make them robust before they ever reach the real world.

This is an early step (and on sports), but we believe it points toward something much bigger: bringing some of the original ideas that made reinforcement learning so powerful back into the physical AI stack.

text:
sharing the full story of how I started Turnkey:

in 2022, i was working at Trade Republic, now the largest neobroker in Europe, where i led the launch of their crypto offering.

at the time, we were evaluating different wallet infrastructure providers and got on a call with one of the bigger names in the industry. the entire process was INSANELY slow.

there were weeks of back and forth, multiple calls, and we couldn’t even get sandbox access until we were deep into the sales process.

i remember leaving those calls thinking to myself that if crypto was actually going to become mainstream, this couldn’t be how developers built products.

wallet infrastructure needed to be:
- self serve & open
- built for developers & easy to integrate
- flexible across use cases

you shouldn’t need weeks of sales calls just to figure out if you a product is going to work for you.

so I realized there was a massive gap in the market. from there things happened fast. my co founder and I put together a deck (peep the old logo on the first slide) about building "Turnkey Wallet Infrastructure," shared it with a few friends to see what they thought, and a week later had a $7.5M term sheet for our seed. 

that became @turnkeyhq.

today, we’ve grown into one of the leading wallet infrastructure providers for companies building crypto and stablecoin products.

if there was 1 piece of advice i could give to founders:

you don't need to lock yourself away to start a company. instead, pay very close attention to the things that frustrate you. if you keep running into the same problem with a vendor, product, or industry process, there’s a good chance others are dealing with it too.

if something feels broken, go build the better version.

We're partnering with @Qualcomm to bring personal AI context to devices powered by Snapdragon. Liquid Context, our on-device context layer, is now optimized for Snapdragon processors and runs on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

Our goal: Give the agents people choose an understanding of what matters to them and when they need help. With the user's permission, Liquid Context learns from device signals and builds an understanding of their routines, preferences, and needs. That understanding is built and maintained locally, and Liquid Context shares relevant context with the user's chosen agents, whether they run on the device, in the cloud, or across both. That includes third-party agents and Liquid Agent, our efficient embedded agent powered by LFM2.5-2.6B.

Running on the Hexagon NPU, Liquid Context works in the background and keeps that understanding current without requiring a cloud model to process every update.

For device manufacturers, this is a path to add personal context to their devices while supporting their own choice of agents and services. OEMs building embedded or hybrid agents can also work with us to evaluate Liquid Agent.

As our CEO @ramin_m_h said: "Personal AI starts with understanding how you live and what you need, when you need it. Liquid Context builds that understanding on your device so the agents you choose can offer more relevant help and anticipate your needs."

text:
Revisiting this essay because - aside from being beautifully written - it speaks to opportunities I find most exciting from a capital allocation point-of-view.

To premise, the macro picture is changing fast. What we thought was the "risk-free" rate is quickly becoming unstable. The bedrock of credit is growing shakier by the day.

Central banks have been piling into the gold the last few years as trust in the dollar erodes. The reaction to return to the sound money that has worked for thousands of years is completely warranted.

However, we live in the 21st century. Tech solutions only become better, faster, and more personalized. Physical solutions to money become strained if our ambition is to expand into the stars - not to mention the possibility of synthetically creating the materials we find valuable (gold doesn't have this problem yet, but it could).

The logical conclusion is sound digital money, one that is true everywhere always, and can be transferred at the higher physical barrier of the speed of light. Once we've established the digital vehicle for value transfer, we can financialize and build capital markets.

In doing so, digitization of the physical world unlocks sources of nuanced yield potentially uncorrelated to traditional assets - a Cambrian explosion of different assets to allocate to. These are assets tethered to more niche areas of the physical world that haven't been financialized yet - now made possible in the new medium.

For an allocator with a wealth preservation mandate, these assets deserve serious analysis as they continue to grow. Frontier Yield can come from anywhere, all at once.

My first piece for @NewYorker is out today!

As Xi Jinping lands in DC to start his state visit, you'll hear a lot about the US-China AI race. I'd like to tell a complementary AI story.

This past May, a few days after Trump visited Beijing, I went to the town people call China's vibe-coding capital, Liangzhu. There, you learn that China's AI scene is not monolithic. It's also full of contrarians, cool vibe coders, spiritual seekers, and people who love AI but refuse to join the 996 grind.

Liangzhu is on the edge of Hangzhou. I hung out with a group of anti-mainstream builders who use AI to make whimsical apps for fortune-telling, mental well-being, and creativity. Some of them run their lives entirely by bazi astrology (their founder almost became a Taoist monk). They meet on "Crazy Thursday" to vibe-code together. Rent is cheap, so they can get a bigger place with a living room to have friends over (unthinkable in Beijing or Shenzhen). In Liangzhu, they want to use AI to forge their own future.

It’s a ground-level story—less about model capabilities, hyperscalers, or AI policy, and more about how people in China are using AI, and the human stories behind it.

The product is already live as a capped mainnet demo using real BTC + real USDC, with limits on how much BTC can be used as collateral.

I also compared the current UX with Babylon. I noticed that Babylon’s flow has more setup and signing steps before the vault is usable.
